binders: A type Ω equipped with a measurable-space structure.
A measure μ on Ω equipped with the structure of a probability measure.
hypotheses: X is integrable with respect to μ.
conclusions: The μ-integral of X equals the Lebesgue integral over t > 0 of μ({ω | t < X(ω)}), minus the Lebesgue integral over t < 0 of μ({ω | X(ω) < t}).
mathematical_definitions: The integral ∫ X dμ is the real-valued Bochner integral, hence the expectation of X under the probability measure μ.
The first threshold integral is ∫_(0,∞) μ(X > t) dt.
The second threshold integral is ∫_(-∞,0) μ(X < t) dt.
Both threshold integrals use Lebesgue measure restricted to the indicated open half-line.
The set measure μ.real(A) is the real number obtained from the extended-nonnegative-real value μ(A).
translation.proposition_plain_english: For every integrable measurable real-valued random variable X on a probability space, its expectation equals the integral of its upper-tail probabilities over positive thresholds minus the integral of its lower-tail probabilities over negative thresholds.

restrictions_and_vacuity_risks: The statement applies only when μ is a probability measure.
The statement assumes X is everywhere measurable, which is stronger than merely being almost-everywhere measurable.
The statement assumes X is integrable, excluding random variables with non-finite absolute expectation.
The tail events use strict inequalities, and the threshold domains exclude 0; these endpoint choices do not alter the Lebesgue integrals but are part of the exact formal statement.
MeasureTheory.Measure.real uses ENNReal.toReal, which would map an infinite measure value non-faithfully; the probability-measure assumption prevents tail-event measures from being infinite.
No vacuity risk is apparent: probability spaces and measurable integrable real-valued functions exist.
